newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Next shares slip after profit rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Next shares slip after profit rise.

text.p: British fashion chain Next Plc on Wednesday reported a 27 percent rise in first half profits, but its shares fell on fears that it may have missed out on a summer spending boom.
Pretax profits in the first half rose to 56 million pounds ($87.11 million), the top of market expectations.
But disappointment with sales growth in the second half took the gloss off the results and hit the shares, which fell 29 pence to 571 before closing at 574.
Next, one of the few retailers to prosper when consumer demand was in the doldrums, admitted it had not expected such a strong summer spending spree.
Chief executive David Jones said: "With the best will in the world you don't budget for a 23 percent increase in turnover." Next's retail operation raised sales in the first half by 23 percent.
"I think the main mistake we made towards the end of the season was that we were caught short of stock," he told a news conference.

Jones said sales in June and July were well above expectations and Next brought stock forward from August into July leaving it short of stock later. He said it would take a few more weeks to get stock back to where the company wanted.
Next's total sales in the first half rose to 406.4 million pounds from 333.3 million.

But in the five weeks from August 12 sales in the company's stores rose just nine percent on the previous year based on the same amount of selling space. Retail analysts said the rise in second half sales had been slower than forecast.

"The increase in sales is a lot slower than people were expecting," said Nick Bubb, retail analyst at MeesPierson, adding that the market had expected Next to receive a bigger boost from Britain's summer.
"It's still one of the darlings of the stores sector, but it does mean it has lost out a bit," said another retail analyst.

Jones said in an interview that Next was quite relaxed about its 143 million pound cash mountain, which it would use to fund generous dividend payouts and investment in its warehouse reorganisation, due for completion by the end of 1997.
"We don't have to go running to banks to do what we want to do," he said: "We don't feel embarrassed by having 140 odd million."

He dismissed speculation that the appointment of Next chairman Lord Wolfson as chairman of rival Great Universal Stores Plc might lead to a link-up between the two retailers. "I don't really think that there's anything on the horizon at the moment, not as far as I'm aware."
He said Next was happy to see Wolfson remain chairman as long as there was no conflict of interest.

Next is expanding its franchises overseas and will have 30 stores mainly in the Middle East and Far East by the end of the year. But there are no plans to add to its four stores in the United States or to its poorly-performing single French store.

Next recently rejoined Britain's FTSE index of top 100 companies. The group has staged a meteoric recovery since over-expansion in the 1980s retail boom almost brought it to its knees five years ago. ($1=.6428 Pound)
